episodes.209936: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, but precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon. This resulted in a multitude of creeks and rivers to rise out of their banks in southeast Ohio, including the Little Muskingum River and Duck Creek. Local road closures also occurred as a result of nearby creeks and streams rising out of the banks and spilling onto the roadways. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off on March 6th.
episodes.210077: Between the evening of March 3 and the late hours of March 4, 2026, a significant hydrologic event unfolded across central Indiana as a stalled frontal boundary interacted with a highly anomalous moisture profile. Driven by a robust 50-knot low-level jet, precipitable water values surged to nearly 1.30 inches���well above the 90th percentile for early March. While the Storm Prediction Center initially identified a low-probability severe threat, the environment was dominated by deep-layer moisture transport and training convective elements, leading to widespread 48-hour rainfall totals of 4 to 6 inches.
episodes.210213: A stationary front stalled out across Ohio and Indiana, sparking showers and thunderstorms along the boundary. Some of the storms produced locally heavy rainfall, resulting in instances of flash flooding.
episodes.210214: A warm front lifted through the Ohio Valley, sparking thunderstorms in a moist airmass. Some of these storms produced locally heavy rainfall, resulting in flooding and flash flooding.
episodes.210265: An isolated severe thunderstorm produced localized wind damage over Hardy County, WV.
episodes.210284: Severe thunderstorms with large hail fell across portions of southwest Missouri during the morning of March 4th. Additional thunderstorms with large hail fell across southern Missouri during the evening of March 4th. The two rounds of thunderstorms produced a swatch of 2-4 inches of rainfall from Cassville to Springfield to Salem. This rainfall caused localized flooding.
episodes.210812: A slow-moving front and a handful of upper level disturbances brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms to North and Central Texas March 4 through 7, resulting in hail and flash flooding in some cases.
episodes.210973: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 4th, ahead of a cold front moving into the region. The thunderstorms continued to affect the area through the early morning hours of the 5th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to golf ball size.
episodes.210997: On the night of the 3rd and 4th of March, an upper level system moved in to the combined Panhandles sparking a line of thunderstorms running southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle. The southern most storm developed into a severe storm that dropped hail up to 2 in diameter across Potter and Randall County.  On the evening of the 5th of March increase moisture advection in the southeastern Panhandles provided instability for severe thunderstorms. This time in the southeastern Panhandles. One of these storms dropped hail up to 1.7 in Collingsworth County.
episodes.211101: A stationary boundary from around Fayetteville to St. Louis to Indianapolis remained throughout the 4th, with the Quad State positioned in the warm sector. A WNW to ESE oriented band of thunderstorms tracked northeastward late evening with hail up to half dollar size falling in Pope County. At the Dixon Springs Agricultural Center, hail shattered a dozen windows and damaged high tunnels while damaging winds blew down multiple trees. MLCAPE values were down to around 250J/kg but 30-40kts of effective bulk shear was sufficient to produce severe storms.
episodes.211102: A stationary boundary from around Fayetteville to St. Louis to Indianapolis remained throughout the 4th, with the Quad State positioned in the warm sector. A WNW to ESE oriented band of thunderstorms tracked northeastward late evening with hail reported in Southeast Missouri. MLCAPE values were around 500J/kg with 30-40kts of effective bulk shear.
episodes.211103: Training of moderate to heavy rain overnight the 4th into the 5th resulted in observed rainfall amounts of 1-2 in Southern Illinois with locally higher amounts up to 5.5 in far Southern Illinois. Flash flooding was observed in Union and Pope Counties. Precipitable water values were 1.3-1.4. The highest observed rainfall totals were 5.51 at CoCoRaHS site IL-PL-2 in Pulaski County, 5.32 at the Dixon Springs mesonet site DSFI2, and 4.02 at the Dongola mesonet site DNGLA.
episodes.211104: Periods of moderate to heavy rain overnight the 4th into the 5th resulted in observed rainfall amounts up to 2 in Southwest Indiana. Ponding of water on roads occurred in Evansville as a result. Precipitable water values were 1.3-1.4.
episodes.211105: Periods of moderate to heavy rain overnight the 4th into the 5th resulted in observed rainfall amounts of 1-2.25 in northern portions of Western Kentucky. Standing water resulted in closure of several roads in Western Kentucky. Flash flooding was observed in Crittenden County. Precipitable water values were 1.2-1.3. The lone severe thunderstorm damaged the roof of a building in Princeton.
episodes.211106: Training of moderate to heavy rain overnight the 4th into the 5th resulted in observed rainfall amounts of 1-3 in northern portions of Southeast Missouri, with locally higher values of 3-4.5 in parts of Perry, Bollinger, and Cape Girardeau Counties. Flash flooding was observed near Perryville and Cape Girardeau. Precipitable water values were 1.3-1.4. Two CoCoRaHS gages observed 4.45 and 4.35 in Cape Girardeau County, while COOP and CoCoRaHS sites in Perry County observed 4.10 and 4.00 respectively.
episodes.211198: After record dry conditions over winter, torrential rainfall on the 4th-5th in upstream portions of the St. Francis River resulted in minor flooding of the river at Patterson, with water levels falling back below flood stage on the 6th. Flooding impacts were limited to minor low-lying and agricultural areas.
episodes.211200: After very dry conditions over winter, multiple rounds of heavy rainfall the first week of March across Indiana resulted in moderate flooding along the White River at Petersburg and Hazleton, with flooding lasting just over two weeks. Flooding affected agricultural areas, oil wells, and several low-lying county roads.
episodes.211257: Approximately 24 hours of near constant rainfall produced 2 to 5 inches of rain in southeast Missouri. This amount of rainfall caused Flat Creek to rise above its banks where it spilled into a nearby neighborhood. Evacuations were required, but no injuries or fatalities were reported.
episodes.211265: A warm front lifted through the Ohio Valley, prompting showers and thunderstorms in a warm and moist airmass. Some storms produced locally heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding and high water.
episodes.211830: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed ahead of cold front extending from North Texas into Southeast Oklahoma during the evening of March 4th. Storm organization and mid-level rotation was noted with individual cells in the vicinity of the cold front as it shifted east along the Red River. Effective shear of 30-40 knots and MLCAPE of 1500-2000 J/kg was sufficient to support occasional supercells across the region, with an increasing coverage of storms in response to an associated mid-level shortwave trough ejecting eastward and coupled with a modest strengthening of the low-level jet. One supercell thunderstorm in particular resulted in localized damaging wind gusts in the Sherwood community east of U.S. Highway 259 in McCurtain County Oklahoma, snapping a few pine trees in this area.
episodes.212440: An outflow boundary from a collapsed thunderstorm moved west over Gulf of America waters north of Big Pine Key, producing isolated gale-force wind gusts.

Emergency management reported multiple water rescues were ongoing at both High Pointe Ln and Brookside Drive.
Emergency management reported multiple cars stranded in water in Cedar Hill near Hillside Village and Uptown.
Broadcast media reported 1.25 inch hail near Joe Pool Lake.
Emergency manager sent images of measured 1.5 inch hail at HWY 171 and CR 304.
A trained spotter reported 1 inch hail at FM 4 and CR 305.
Heavy rains washed out a bridge on County Road 1100 North at Wolf Creek.
Quarter size hail was measured in East Prairie as a storm tracked northeastward into Mississippi County.
A social media image showed measured 1.75 inch to 2 inch hailstones near Mineral Wells.
Mping report of 2 inch hail near Mineral Wells.
Estimated hail size, reported via mPING.

events.narrative: An east wind of 34 knots was measured at a WeatherFlow station at Harbor Bank Light.
Hail to the size of quarters fell west of Eagle Rock.

The fire department reported multiple houses were flooding on Pecan Ave in Wills Point. Local FD requested a boat and were going door to door evacuating residents. Four to five feet of water was prohibiting egress on foot.
Wills Point FD reported SH 64 just south of the airport was not passable and has been blocked off.
Large hail up to golf ball size damaged homes and vehicles.
Emergency manager reported multiple main roads in Balch Springs were flooded with stranded motorists. Several houses had water of an unknown depth inside. Numerous side streets were also flooded.

The fire department reported knee deep water over Highway 80 near Big Tex Trailers at the Wills Point city limit. Wills Point Fire and Edgewood Fire were working multiple calls for flooding of stranded occupants in vehicles on Highway 80.
Several vehicles were stranded in high water, requiring multiple water rescues along Eaton Road, near Seven Mile.
A few snapped softwood trees were reported in the Sherwood community east of Highway 259.

Multiple large trees were downed by downburst winds at the Dixon Springs Ag Center. Hail of unknown size shattered over a dozen windows and damaged all three high tunnels and the greenhouse. For the tunnels, the plastic was riddled with indentations and one of the three tunnels was torn. For the greenhouse, the polycarbonate sheets were described as Swiss cheese.
High water was reported over several roadways and was approaching structures in Millville.
Social media pictures showed hail measured to quarter to half-dollar size near Eddyville.
Over a foot of standing water inundated at least eleven cars at a local car dealer and portions of the corner gas station. Several homes also had water over their porches, up to their front doors.

Indian Creek came out of its banks and inundated the basement and first floor of a home near the intersection of Walnut Street and Ross Hanover Road. A swift water rescue was needed to remove the family from the home.
Emergency manager reported quarter size hail near Lake Kiowa.
Multiple cars were stranded in high water along Germantown Road, under a railroad crossing.

Two to five inches of rain fell in St. Francois county in about 24 hours ending on March 5th. This rain caused Flat Creek to rise above its banks as far east as Garrett St and as far west as Camilla St. A few evacuations were required as water approached homes in these areas. Water receded by 4am.
Several feet of water was reported to be flowing over Warwick Road.
Highway 63 was closed due to flooding just north of Highway 72 underneath a railroad bridge in Rolla.
State Highway H was closed due to flooding near Black Oak Creek.
Multiple roads were closed due to flash flooding in Perryville as 3-hr rainfall rates reached estimated totals of 2.5.
State Highway TT was closed due to flooding near Crooked Creek.
Flash flooding occurred in Cape Girardeau with several roads flooded early morning. Multiple buildings had some water intrusion on the Southeast Missouri State University campus.
Water was observed on road at State Route 56 and Huggins Road. State Route 328 was closed from State Route 93 to State Route 56 due to flooding from Racoon Creek.

Duck Creek at Macksburg rose above a bankfull level of 13 feet on the morning of March 5th, then continued to rise to a crest around 14.5 feet that afternoon. The creek plateaued and then receded back below bankfull level the next morning. While the creek was out of its banks, flooding of the campground next to the gauge, Broad Street, Main Street, and fields and low-lying areas adjacent to the creek occurred.

IL-145 was closed due to flash flooding between Glendale and Dixon Springs. The mesonet station DSFI2 at Dixon Springs recorded 5.32 inches of rain in a 24hr period ending at 700CST with most of the rainfall occurring after midnight.

Water covered roads southeast of Old Appleton. Radar estimated rainfall from midnight through the early morning hours was approximately 3 inches in the area. To the southwest, there was a 24-hr rainfall report at 700CST of 4.35in at a CoCoRaHS site 1WSW of Oak Ridge.

Lingle Creek flooded out of its banks, washing out the road. Radar estimated rainfall at this location overnight through the early morning approached half a foot. A mesonet station in Dongola reported 4.02in of rain through early morning.

Lingering road closures continued into the morning in Perryville. 24hr rainfall totals ending 700CST on the 5th reached 4.10in at a CoCoRaHS site 1mi NE of Perryville and 4.00in at the PRRM7 COOP site at the Perryville Water Treatment Plant.
Levee Road was closed due to high water. Several additional roads were closed due to high water in the vicinity.
Water covered 3/4 of the roadway on KY-136E at US-41.
State Highway Z was closed due to flooding north of Hartville.
State Highway AB was closed due to flooding northeast of Mansfield.
Areas of high water were reported over the roadway between E County Road 1400 N and IN-229.
High water on roads resulted in the closure of KY-285 between MM1.6 and MM3.6.
Water covered parts of roads near Corydon.
Portions of KY-132 (MM11-11.2 and 12-13) and KY-1340 (MM0-1) were closed due to high water.
A portion of KY-283 (MM2.1-2.4) was closed due to high water.

Heavy rainfall during the early morning of the 5th resulted in several spots in northeastern Crittenden County with damage to roads including gravel washing out on small sections of Blackford Church Rd, Caney Fork Rd, and Cool Springs Rd. Radar estimated rainfall was only around two inches in total though an inch or so fell between 1130-1215CST.
An approximately 20-30ft section of a metal roof was blown off of an industrial building in Princeton as a thunderstorm tracked eastward through the city during the early morning.
Anderson Road east of State Route 380 was closed due to high water over the road.
High water over the roadway caused Waynesville Jamestown Road to be closed just east of State Route 68.
Armbrust Road near Flakesford Road SW was closed due to high water over the road.
A picture on Facebook showed several inches of swiftly moving water across Mexico Rd.
Standing water of approximately six to eight inches was observed in downtown Evansville. Observed rainfall totals through the early morning reached two inches in the area.

Sunday Creek at Glouster rose above a bankfull level of 13 feet on the morning of March 5th, then continued to rise to a crest near 15.1 feet that evening. The creek then slowly receded back below bankfull level the next morning. Flooding took place in many locations, including the Trimble High School parking lot, Center Street and Route 13 near Congress Street in Trimble, Palmer Street in Jacksonville, and West Main Street, portions of Oakdale Road, South Town Street, Kennedy Road, and Glouster Memorial Park in Glouster.
Waterloo Road NW had high water over the roadway between Winchester Road NW and Hill Road.
Leitnaker Road NE between Old Millersport Road NE and State Route 37 had high water over the roadway.
Flooding issues lingered into the morning in the city of Cape Girardeau. Storm total rainfall at a CoCoRaHS site 1ESE of Cape Girardeau was 4.45in.
State Route 668 was flooded at Dutch Ridge Road about a mile south of Maxville.
State Route 56 East was closed beyond Dogwood Ridge Road to State Route 356 due to flooding from Hewett Fork.
State Highway NN was closed due to flooding at Rocky Creek.
Sugar Creek was out of its banks, resulting in about a foot of water flowing over Bush Road NW.

The Little Muskingum River at Bloomfield rose above a bankfull level of 16 feet on the morning of March 5th, then continued to rise to a crest around 22.4 feet that night. The river then slowly receded back below bankfull level the next morning. While the river was out of its banks, flooding of fields next to the river and Route 26 near the intersection with Route 260 took place.
State Highway Y was closed due to flooding west of Ava.
High water was reported over Port William-Lumberton Road in between Bone Road and Faulkner Road.
High water was reported over Hale's Branch Road between Jonesboro Road and Cochran Road.
Day Lane in Christian county was closed due to flooding.
Keltner Road in Christian County was closed due to flooding.
Buck Road in Christian County was closed due to flooding.
Wilson Road was closed due to flooding.
Frost Road was closed between Smith Road and Rome Township Road 532 due to flooding.
Baker Road was closed between Marion Johnson Road and Enlow Road due to flooding from Dirty Creek.
Carbondale Road was closed between Waterloo Township Road 444 and Dowler Ridge Road due to flooding.
Potter Road was closed due to flooding from Wyatt Run and McDougall Branch.
Jacksonville Road was closed between Dover Township Road 583 and Wemmer Road due to flooding.
State Highway U was closed due to flooding.
State Highway 95 was closed due to flooding.
S Cave Hill Road was closed due to high water for about two miles between S County Road 350 E and IN-62.

Duck Creek below Whipple rose above a bankfull level of 12 feet on the afternoon of March 5th, then continued to rise to a crest near 14.3 feet during the night. The creek then slowly receded back below bankfull level the afternoon of the 6th. While the creek was out of its banks, flooding of low sections of Route 821 below Whipple, the intersection of Kohl and Whipple Run Roads, Route 16 above Stanleyville, and fields next to the creek and around Whipple occurred.
West Main Street flooded under the railroad overpass.
State Route 56 had high water reported over the roadway.
State Route 56 had high water over multiple locations including near Creamery Hill Road as well as near Big Pine Road.

Water levels briefly rose several feet into minor flood on the St. Francis River at Patterson, cresting at 21.40ft just after midnight on the 6th. Flooding affected mainly bottomland and surrounding low-lying areas.
High water was reported between Gravel Pit Road and Cummings Road.
Flooding was observed on Ridgeland Road neat Keystone Furnace Road due to flooding from Dickason Run.

Moderate flooding occurred on the White River near Petersburg, with river levels cresting at 24.80ft on the 11th. Widespread flooding affected agricultural lands and low oil fields. Several low-lying county roads flooded on the Pike County side. Flooding continued through the middle of the month.
State Highway BB was closed due to flooding along the Big Piney River.
Trees blew down in the 2100 block of CR-7 South Fork Road.
State Highway H was closed due to flooding along the North Fork River.
